name: Cascais
seoTitle: Should You Take the Train to Cascais on a Port Day?
tagline: The easiest seaside trip from the ship, but it needs about six hours ashore.

description.short: Former fishing town and seaside resort at the end of the coastal railway from Lisbon. One walk and one train from the cruise terminal, about 1 hour 15 minutes door to door each way, with no bookings needed.
description.full:
Cascais is a former fishing town turned seaside resort at the end of the coastal railway from Lisbon. It is the simplest day trip from the ship: no bookings, no timed tickets and no hills. Our guide to Cascais and Estoril on a port day covers the journey step by step; this is the short version.

Getting there: walk 26 to 28 minutes west along the river to Cais do Sodré, or take a taxi (about 10 minutes), then the Cascais-line train, which runs roughly every 20 minutes and takes 33 to 40 minutes to the terminus. The single fare is 2.55 euros in 2026. Door to door, allow about 1 hour 15 minutes each way.

Minimum time ashore: 6 hours, which leaves about two and a half hours in town. With 5 to 6 hours it is tight, and only worth it if a beach matters more to you than Lisbon. Under 5 hours, stay in the city.

What to prioritise with two to three hours: the old town lanes and fishing harbour next to the station, the waterfront past the Cidadela to the marina, and Boca do Inferno, a sea chasm about 2 km west (around 20 minutes on foot along a flat road). Lunch on grilled fish near the harbour; a street back from the seafront is usually better value. With an extra hour, get off one station early at Estoril and walk the seafront promenade to Cascais (30 to 40 minutes).

What to skip: Guincho beach and Cabo da Roca need a bus or taxi and eat the time you have. Cabo da Roca by public transport adds 2 to 2.5 hours, so do not attempt it by bus on a call under 9 hours. Skip the museums too: Cascais is an outdoor trip, and in rain it loses most of its appeal.

For a first visit to Lisbon, Cascais is usually not the best use of a port day. It makes sense if you have seen the city before, want a beach and sea air, or the day is hot.
description.history: Cascais grew up as a fishing port and a fortified post guarding the mouth of the Tagus; the 16th-century fortress of Nossa Senhora da Luz and the 17th-century Cidadela still stand on the waterfront. From 1870 King Luís I spent his summers in the Cidadela, and the court and Lisbon's aristocracy followed, building villas along the coast. The railway from Lisbon reached Cascais in 1889 and turned it into the capital's seaside resort. During and after the Second World War, the Estoril coast sheltered refugees, spies and exiled royalty, including Umberto II of Italy and the Spanish pretender Juan de Borbón. Today it is a prosperous commuter town as well as a resort.
description.significance: For a cruise passenger, Cascais is the easiest way to reach the Atlantic coast near Lisbon: one train, a station in the town centre and beaches within a few minutes' walk. The ride is part of the appeal, running beside the Tagus past Belém and then along the open coast. Cascais is also the starting point for Boca do Inferno, Guincho and the bus to Cabo da Roca.

directions.general: Located on the Atlantic coast, 30km west of Lisbon along the Estoril Coast
directions.fromCruisePort: Walk 26 to 28 minutes west along the river to Cais do Sodré station, or take a taxi (about 10 minutes). Cascais-line trains run roughly every 20 minutes and take 33 to 40 minutes to Cascais, the terminus. Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes door to door.
directions.publicTransport: CP Cascais line from Cais do Sodré to Cascais (33-40 minutes, roughly every 20 minutes in the daytime; 2.55 euros single in 2026). Carris Metropolitana bus 1624 runs from the Cascais bus terminal to Cabo da Roca and Portela de Sintra.
directions.parking: Multiple paid parking lots in town center. Free parking available further from center. Limited street parking.

seasonal.hours: Town, beaches and seafront always open; museums, shops and restaurants keep their own hours
seasonal.notes: Bathing season roughly May to September

admissionPrices.notes: Free to visit the town and beaches; museums charge separately. Train Cais do Sodré-Cascais: 2.55 euros single (four zones) or 5.10 euros for the Lisboa-Cascais return ticket on CP's January 2026 price list. The reusable Navegante card costs 0.50 euros.

visitingInformation.averageVisitDuration: 2.5-4 hours in town on a port day
visitingInformation.bestTimeToVisit: A dry, warm day. Weekdays are quieter than summer weekends, when Lisbon residents head for the beaches.
visitingInformation.adviceForVisitors: Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes each way from the ship. Load Zapping credit on a Navegante card to skip the ticket queue at Cais do Sodré. Sit on the left heading out for the river and sea views. Plan the return train backwards from all-aboard.

cruisePassengerInfo.timeNeededFromPort: At least 6 hours ashore (about 1 hour 15 minutes each way plus 2.5 hours in town); 5-6 hours is tight
cruisePassengerInfo.accessibility: Easy: a flat walk or short taxi ride to Cais do Sodré and one train to the terminus, which is in the town centre. The old town has cobbles and some slopes; the town beaches are reached by steps or ramps.
combinableWith: Cabo da Roca (by taxi or driver; by bus only on calls of 9 hours or more)
tips: Buy a reusable Navegante card (0.50 euros) per person and load Zapping credit, so you can skip the ticket queue at Cais do Sodré.
Sit on the left-hand side heading out for views of the Tagus and the coast.
Pick your return train and the one before it; if a train is cancelled, the next is usually about 20 minutes behind.
Board the return train at Cascais, the terminus, to be sure of a seat.
Boca do Inferno is about 20 minutes' walk west on a flat road; stay behind the railings, especially when a swell is running.
For Estoril as well, get off at Estoril, walk the seafront promenade to Cascais (30-40 minutes) and take the train back from Cascais.
The Cascais line is being modernised in 2026, with closures at night and early on Sunday mornings between Caxias and Cascais; check cp.pt the day before.
In rain or fog, stay in Lisbon: Cascais is almost entirely an outdoor visit.

highlights: Old town lanes paved in wave-patterned Portuguese cobbles
Fishing harbour and Praia da Ribeira, next to the station
Praia da Rainha and Praia da Conceição, small sheltered town beaches
Cidadela fortress and the marina on the waterfront
Boca do Inferno sea chasm, about 2 km west of the centre
Museu Condes de Castro Guimarães, an early-20th-century mansion on the road to Boca do Inferno
facilities: Public restrooms in Parque Marechal Carmona
Free WiFi in some public areas

accessibility.mobilityNotes: Town center relatively flat with some wheelchair-accessible routes. Old Town has cobblestones and hills. Some beaches have accessible ramps (Praia da Conceição). Beach clubs may have accessibility features. Trains from Lisbon are accessible. Santa Marta Lighthouse not wheelchair accessible. Coastal walks have uneven terrain.
